analysis.one_liner: Requires stores to let customers with urgent medical needs use employee restrooms.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to a House committee and its Health Subcommittee in July 2023 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required retail stores open to the public to let a customer use an employee-only restroom if the customer has a certified medical condition that demands immediate restroom access, such as Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, an ostomy, or pregnancy. Access would apply only when a public restroom isn't available, at least two employees are on duty, and the restroom isn't in a safety-risk area. The Labor Department would issue ID cards to people whose doctor certifies a qualifying condition.
analysis.who_benefits: People with conditions like inflammatory bowel disease or an ostomy, who can face urgent, unpredictable restroom needs and are sometimes denied access to employee-only restrooms in stores.

how_it_helps.text: Retail establishments with non-public restrooms must allow a customer with an eligible medical condition to use them during business hours when the conditions in the bill are met.

Qualifying conditions include inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or irritable bowel syndrome, use of an ostomy device, pregnancy, or any other diagnosed condition requiring immediate restroom access.

Within 180 days of enactment, the Secretary of Labor would create a system to issue identification cards to people whose medical professional certifies an eligible condition, giving stores a simple way to verify the request.

Safeguards limit the mandate: access is required only when a public restroom is not available, two or more employees are working, and the restroom is not in an area with an obvious health or safety risk.

analysis.who_pays: Retail stores, which would bear a small cost to unlock employee restrooms for verified customers and to accommodate the ID-card verification process; the cost falls mostly on staffing time and restroom upkeep.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail stores open to the public

drawbacks.text: The mandate falls on retail establishments, including small stores, which would have to let strangers into employee-only areas; businesses argue this raises security and safety concerns, though the bill exempts restrooms in areas with obvious health or safety risks and requires two employees on duty.

The bill relies on a new federal ID-card system run by the Labor Department, adding a bureaucratic step: shoppers without a card would have no protection under the bill even with an obvious urgent need.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it protects a specific group of shoppers from a specific, degrading situation at modest cost to stores. The conditions attached (two employees present, no public restroom available, no safety risk, an ID card) keep the burden small, but the ID requirement also limits coverage. A reasonable bill whose cost was small relative to who it helps.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, then to that committee's Health Subcommittee four days later, and neither ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Eleanor Holmes Norton, the Delegate representing Washington, DC, introduced the bill on July 10, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On July 14, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was recorded.
The bill drew 5 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or Senate consideration before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retail stores are better off because the bill died: they face no new obligation to open employee restrooms. Shoppers with urgent medical conditions gained nothing.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Delegate, District of Columbia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on July 10, 2023.

for.name: 5 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans cosponsored it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and took no further action on it; no markup was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all 5 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican acted on the bill in either direction.

industries.note: Had it passed, stores open to the public would have had to allow verified customers with urgent medical needs to use employee restrooms, a small operating cost. Keeping those restrooms off-limits is the practice the bill targets, so retailers' interest ran against the customers the bill serves.
